meta.descriptionEn: Thirty-six seconds after liftoff, a bolt of lightning hit the Saturn V carrying Apollo 12. Fifty-two seconds in, a second strike came. Fuel cells went offline, warning lights lit up the cabin, and Mission Control's data turned to garbage. Nobody knew exactly what was wrong, and the crew was racing skyward on top of a giant rocket. Then a flight controller remembered a strange failure pattern from an earlier test and made a call that sounded like nonsense to most of the room. Would the mission be aborted? Was the spacecraft damaged beyond repair? And how did the crew still go on to make a pinpoint landing beside a probe that had sat on the Moon for two and a half years? Discover the full story of Apollo 12.
meta.descriptionUr: Apollo 12 ke launch ke sirf 36 second baad bijli Saturn V rocket par gir gayi, aur 52 second par doosri baar. Fuel cells band ho gaye, cabin mein warning lights jal gayin aur Mission Control ka data bekaar ho gaya. Kisi ko samajh nahi aa raha tha ke masla kya hai. Phir ek flight controller ko purana ek test yaad aaya aur usne aisi call di jo bohat se logon ko ajeeb lagi. Kya mission abort ho jata? Kya spacecraft ko bara nuksan pohancha tha? Aur crew ne Moon par Surveyor 3 ke bilkul qareeb landing kaise ki? Poori kahani is documentary mein dekhein, Urdu aur English mein.

articleEn: On 14 November 1969, rain was falling in Florida as the Apollo 12 Saturn V rocket climbed into the sky. Everything was going smoothly. Then, 36.5 seconds after liftoff, lightning struck the rocket directly. All three fuel cells suddenly dropped offline, leaving the spacecraft running on batteries alone. At 52 seconds, a second strike hit. This time the 8-ball attitude indicator went dark too, another key instrument silenced.

In Mission Control, the telemetry screens showed garbled data. In front of the astronauts, the whole board of caution and warning lights glowed red. Yet they did not know exactly where the fault lay. Oddly, the Saturn V kept flying perfectly well.

So the questions piled up. Which switch could put everything right? Why did the rocket keep flying while the spacecraft's power faltered? And the biggest question of all: could this mission still reach the Moon, or would it have to be ended immediately? The answer, as it turns out, lay in one small switch. Let's go back to the beginning and see the whole story of Apollo 12.

articleEn: Today Apollo 12 is often overshadowed by Apollo 11. But it was the sixth crewed flight of the Apollo program and the second mission to land on the Moon. NASA launched it on 14 November 1969 from Kennedy Space Center in Florida, and on 19 November it landed in the Moon's Ocean of Storms.

There is an interesting detail about this mission. Had Apollo 11 failed, Apollo 12 would have made the first attempt at a Moon landing. In other words, Apollo 12 held the backup plan for the first landing, and both crews had trained for the same landing sites. But Apollo 11 succeeded. The pressure eased, and Apollo 12 was postponed by two months. The schedule of the other Apollo missions was also relaxed somewhat, so the rush that had come before the first landing was gone.

Geology training benefited from this extra time. Conrad and Bean spent more time learning geology than the Apollo 11 crew had, and took many field trips. The spacecraft and launch vehicle were much like Apollo 11's. One addition was hammocks, so that Conrad and Bean could lie down comfortably during their stay on the Moon. The two would descend to the lunar surface in the Lunar Module, while Richard Gordon remained in orbit around the Moon with the Command Module. Their combined activity on the surface lasted a little over a day and seven hours.

All of it revolved around one particular target: Surveyor 3, a robotic probe that had landed on the Moon on 20 April 1967. The plan was for Apollo 12 to land within walking distance of it. If that worked, NASA could plan future missions in the hope that astronauts could land close to places of scientific interest.
But wait. Only moments after launch, this whole plan was in danger, and the story that follows is tied to that moment.

articleEn: Now let us meet the crew caught up in the lightning incident. All three astronauts came from the US Navy, making this an all-Navy crew. The commander was Charles "Pete" Conrad. He was 39 at the time of the mission and held an aeronautical engineering degree from Princeton. After Princeton he became a naval aviator and went through the Test Pilot School at Patuxent River. He was selected in NASA's second astronaut group in 1962. Conrad made his first flight on Gemini 5 in 1965 and became command pilot of Gemini 11 in 1966. He stood about 5 feet 6 inches, so Gemini's cramped capsule bothered him less, and he joked that the Gemini 5 capsule was a flying garbage can. This light-hearted manner comes up again later.

Command Module Pilot Richard Gordon was 40. He studied chemistry at the University of Washington and became a naval aviator in 1953. Gordon became an astronaut in 1963 and had flown with Conrad on Gemini 11, so the two had already worked together in space.

The story of the third seat is a sad one. The original Lunar Module Pilot was Clifton Williams, who died in October 1967 in a T-38 jet crash near Tallahassee. Conrad had already wanted Alan Bean, who had been his student at test pilot school. But Deke Slayton, director of Flight Crew Operations, said Bean was unavailable because of his Apollo Applications Program assignment. After Williams died, Conrad asked for Bean again, and this time Slayton agreed. Bean was 37, and Apollo 12 was his first spaceflight. He had studied aeronautical engineering at the University of Texas in 1955.

Interestingly, the three had also served as the Apollo 9 backup crew. The backup crew consisted of David Scott, Alfred Worden and James Irwin, who later became the crew of Apollo 15. Apollo also had a third group besides prime and backup, the support crew. For Apollo 12 it was Gerald Carr, Edward Gibson and Paul Weitz. Slayton created this group because McDivitt felt that preparations were underway across the US and that many meetings would have no member of the flight crew present.

Mission Control had four flight directors: Griffin, Frank, Charlesworth and Windler. The CAPCOMs included Scott, Worden, Irwin, Carr, Gibson, Weitz and Don Lind. And soon the moment would come that would test them all, when lightning struck the rocket.

articleEn: So where would Apollo 12 land? The Apollo 11 site requirements were strict: near the equator, flat ground, and no obstacles along the approach. When Apollo 11 succeeded, the first idea was for Apollo 12 to land at the next site to the west, Sinus Medii. But the planners in Houston thought differently. Jack Sevier and the Houston engineers wanted the landing near the crater where Surveyor 3 had landed in 1967, so the astronauts could bring back parts of it.

The problem was that Apollo 11 had landed several miles from its target. Some NASA administrators feared that if Apollo 12 also landed far off, the agency's reputation would suffer. Yet without pinpoint landing, further exploration was not possible. So on 25 July 1969, Apollo Program Manager Samuel Phillips chose the Surveyor crater. Remarkably, the members of both site selection boards were unanimously against the decision, but it stood.

Next, Surveyor 3 had to be found on the Moon. NASA called in Ewen Whitaker, who had worked on Moon atlases. He examined images of thousands of similar craters under a microscope, then identified two rocks near the probe, which revealed its location. When it landed on 20 April 1967, the radar was confused by shiny rocks. The engines did not shut off, and Surveyor 3 bounced twice. The third time it settled down gently. Its scoop dug four trenches in the lunar soil, and its camera sent back 6,315 pictures to Earth. After the first lunar night it did not wake again.

Now look at the training. Conrad and Bean spent five hours of mission training for every hour of flight, more than 1,000 hours for each astronaut. Conrad flew the Lunar Landing Training Vehicle, even though Armstrong had bailed out of a similar machine in 1968. There were also six geology field trips. Conrad said there would be no publicity or media. On the Apollo 11 field trip, a press helicopter had meant the astronauts could not hear each other. Scientists kept changing the method of photo documentation. After the fourth or fifth change, Conrad demanded there be no more.

Saturn V SA-507 and the spacecraft were much like Apollo 11's. The CSM call sign was Yankee Clipper and the Lunar Module's was Intrepid, both chosen by the Navy crew. There were small changes too. Two hammocks were fitted in the LM for rest, and a color TV camera replaced Apollo 11's black and white one. One important item was ALSEP, a set of scientific instruments. It was powered by a nuclear generator called SNAP-27, which contained plutonium. This was the first use of atomic energy on a crewed NASA spacecraft. So after all this preparation, would everything go smoothly at launch?

articleEn: At last launch day came, 14 November 1969, at Kennedy Space Center, and Apollo 12 stood ready to fly that same day. This time there was a special guest. President Richard Nixon was the first sitting U.S. president to watch a crewed space launch. Vice President Spiro Agnew was there too. Apollo 12 was to lift off at 11:22 am EST, or 16:22 UTC, and the launch window was three hours and four minutes. The window existed so that lighting at the planned landing point would be at its best. If the launch could not happen in that time, there would be a wait.

The Saturn V had no major changes from Apollo 11, only 17 additional instrumentation measurements. The problem was the weather. The sky was covered in clouds and it was raining. During the climb, winds of 151.7 knots were encountered, the strongest of any Apollo mission. NASA's rule was not to launch into a cumulonimbus cloud. That rule was waived. It was later found that the vehicle never actually flew through such a cloud.

What would have happened if the mission had been postponed? A launch could have happened on 16 November, but the landing would have been at a backup site where Surveyor was not present. With the success of Apollo 11, the pressure to reach the Moon quickly was over, so NASA might even have waited until December for the Surveyor crater. In other words, stopping the launch that day was possible. But it was not stopped. Apollo 12 flew at the scheduled time, and the Saturn V stood ready in the rain.

And here is a strange thing. Later investigation found the vehicle had not entered any cumulonimbus, yet lightning still struck, because the vehicle itself triggered it. So did the rocket cause the lightning itself? Yes, and everything was about to change in less than a minute.

articleEn: Now let us move to that moment. 36.5 seconds after liftoff, lightning struck the Saturn V, triggered by the vehicle itself. A static discharge produced a voltage transient that took all three of the spacecraft's fuel cells offline. The spacecraft was now running on batteries alone, and the batteries could not supply as much current as was demanded. Things were getting worse quickly for the crew.

Then at 52 seconds a second strike came. It also knocked out the 8-ball attitude indicator, the instrument that shows which way the spacecraft is oriented. Suddenly the astronauts' whole board lit up red with caution and warning lights, but they could not tell what the real fault was. Imagine it: red lights everywhere, and the crew not knowing exactly what had failed. And the rocket had not been off the ground even a minute.

In Mission Control the picture was no better. The telemetry stream was garbled, meaning the data on the screens looked meaningless. That data passed through the CSM's signal conditioning electronics before reaching the consoles. When the lightning hit, this system was disrupted and nothing on the screens was clear.

But one thing was working perfectly. The Saturn V kept flying its normal path. The reason was that the rocket's Instrument Unit guidance system worked independently of the CSM, and the lightning did not affect it. So the rocket was fine, but the spacecraft on top of it, with its three astronauts, had become a puzzle. The whole launch vehicle had 1,365 instrumentation measurements, but the stream from the spacecraft was tangled, and every second the rocket climbed higher.

All eyes were now on Mission Control's decision makers. Flight Director Gerald Griffin and CAPCOM Gerald Carr did not know about this obscure switch, nor did Commander Conrad. Would the mission end right there? Would Apollo 12 have to abort? Time was running out. One man had seen this pattern before. His seat was at the EECOM console in Mission Control, and his name was John Aaron.

chapters.covers: John Aaron (EECOM) remembered the failure pattern from an earlier test, call 'Flight, EECOM. Try SCE to Aux'; switch obscure, Conrad, Griffin and Carr did not know it; Bean found and threw it, telemetry returned, Bean put fuel cells back online. Earth parking orbit checks, no serious damage. Hidden fear about explosive bolts for the parachute compartment, decision not to tell the crew, parachutes worked at the end.

articleEn: John Aaron had seen the garbled telemetry pattern before. In an earlier test, a power loss had caused a fault in the CSM's signal conditioning electronics. The SCE was the part that turns raw instrumentation signals into data that can be shown on Mission Control's consoles. And Aaron knew the fix too. He said: "Flight, EECOM. Try SCE to Aux." That meant switching the SCE to its backup power supply.

The problem was that this switch was quite obscure. Flight Director Gerald Griffin, CAPCOM Gerald Carr and Conrad himself did not know which switch it was. But inside the spacecraft was someone who knew where it was: Alan Bean, who as Lunar Module Pilot was also an engineer of the spacecraft. Bean found the switch and threw it. After that, telemetry came back online, and the data showed no major malfunction. Then Bean put the fuel cells back online, and the mission went on.

Think about it: one obscure switch, and the timely actions of Aaron and Bean helped save the mission. According to the record, switching to the auxiliary power supply solved the data relay problem, and that helped rescue the mission. The crew was now in Earth parking orbit. They checked the spacecraft very carefully, because after lightning strikes every system mattered. Then preparations began to reignite the S-IVB third stage. It was later found that the lightning strikes had caused no serious permanent damage.

But the story does not end there. There was another worry that was kept from the crew. It concerned the Command Module's parachutes. At first there was concern that the lightning strike might have damaged the explosive bolts that open the Command Module's parachute compartment. It was decided not to tell the astronauts. Since an abort would have gained nothing if the parachutes would not open, the flight plan continued. At the end of the mission the parachutes deployed in a completely normal way, so the hidden fear never became real.
So the crew was about to head for the Moon. But had the Lunar Module of Conrad and Bean also come through the lightning unharmed?

articleEn: After the systems checks, the S-IVB performed the trans-lunar injection burn. It happened at mission time 02:47:22.80 and sent Apollo 12 toward the Moon. An hour and twenty minutes later the CSM separated from the S-IVB. Dick Gordon then performed the transposition, docking and extraction maneuver and pulled the Lunar Module out of that stage. An attempt was made to send the S-IVB toward solar orbit. This time the stage fired its own engines, whereas on Apollo 11 the SPS engine had been used.

The stage's own story is different, though. Because of an error it passed the Moon at a very high altitude and failed to reach Earth escape velocity. It left Earth orbit in 1971. Thirty-one years later it returned temporarily to Earth orbit, and amateur astronomer Bill Yeung discovered it. It was given the temporary name J002E3, and it was then found to be an artificial object. As of 2021 it was in solar orbit, and Earth cannot capture it before the 2040s.

Now to the Lunar Module. Since lightning might have damaged the LM, Conrad and Bean went inside it on the first day to look at its condition. They found no issues. During the translunar coast only one necessary midcourse correction was made. It put Apollo 12 on a hybrid, non-free-return trajectory. Earlier crewed missions had gone to lunar orbit on a free-return trajectory, on which the spacecraft could return easily to Earth even if the engine did not fire. This gave flexibility in planning. Apollo 12 could launch in daylight and reach the landing spot on schedule, though the trip took 8 hours longer.

Then Apollo 12 entered orbit around the Moon at 170.2 by 61.66 nautical miles. On the third revolution a burn made the orbit nearly circular, at 66.1 by 54.59 nautical miles. On the next revolution, preparations for landing began. The CSM and LM undocked at 107:54:02.3, and now Conrad and Bean faced the landing.

articleEn: Now came the landing. After a 29-second Descent Propulsion System burn, the LM entered a lower orbit, and then a 717-second powered descent began. In training, Conrad had been told that at pitchover he would see a pattern of craters, called the Snowman, with the Surveyor crater in the middle. But they feared nothing might be recognizable. Then they were amazed, because the Snowman was exactly where it should be. Conrad took manual control. He wanted to land in Pete's Parking Lot, as in the simulations, but the spot was rougher than expected, so he had to maneuver.

Finally the LM Intrepid landed at 110:32:36.2, which was 06:54:36 UTC on 19 November 1969. The Surveyor probe was only 535 feet, or 163 meters, away. It was a precision landing, and that was one of the mission's major goals. The landing coordinates were 3.01239° S and 23.42157° W, in Oceanus Procellarum, the Ocean of Storms. It is the largest lunar plain, about 4,000,000 km2, or 10.5% of the Moon's surface. Besides Surveyor 3, Luna 9, Luna 13 and Surveyor 1 also landed in Oceanus Procellarum, but humans reached only Surveyor 3. The sandblasting from the landing affected Surveyor. It was later found that it had removed more dust than it deposited, so the surfaces returned toward their original color.

When Conrad stepped onto the lunar surface, he said, "Whoopie! Man, that may have been a small one for Neil, but that's a long one for me." The line was no accident. Conrad had bet journalist Oriana Fallaci 500 dollars; she believed NASA had written Armstrong's words. Then Bean carried the color camera and unknowingly pointed it straight at the Sun. The SEC tube burned out and television coverage ended immediately.

On the first EVA they set up the ALSEP. The RTG's plutonium fuel element would not come out of its cask, so they had to hit the cask with a hammer. On the second EVA the first stop was Head crater. There Bean saw light material beneath Conrad's footprints, a sign of ejecta from Copernicus crater. Then they reached the Surveyor crater. They descended carefully, but the ground was firm and the probe was stable. They cut off several parts, including Surveyor 3's television camera, and took them. There is also a small story: the two had brought an automatic timer, without telling Mission Control, to take a selfie, but it could not be found among the Hand Tool Carrier's samples.

The first EVA lasted 3 hours 56 minutes 3 seconds and the second 3 hours 49 minutes 15 seconds. The second covered 4,300 feet, and a total of 73.75 pounds of samples were collected. In this way Apollo 12 showed that NASA could plan future missions to land near places of scientific interest. But the return was still ahead.

articleEn: While Conrad and Bean were on the lunar surface, Dick Gordon circled alone in orbit. He carried out the Lunar Multispectral Photography Experiment with four Hasselblad cameras, each fitted with a filter of a different color. This allowed an estimate of the composition of sites that humans would not reach soon. On 20 November 1969 Intrepid lifted off from the Moon. About three and a half hours later the LM and Command Module docked again. The LM's ascent stage was then separated. Controlled from Earth, it was crashed into the Moon and hit 39 nautical miles from the landing point. The seismometer left on the Moon recorded the shaking from the impact for more than an hour. The impact was also planned to help calibrate the seismometer.

The crew stayed in orbit for another day, taking pictures. Then Yankee Clipper made its trans-Earth injection burn, which lasted a little over 130 seconds. On the way home, the Earth passed in front of the Sun. Pictures of this solar eclipse were taken, and according to Bean it was the most spectacular sight of the whole mission. On 24 November 1969 Yankee Clipper splashed down in the South Pacific, southeast of Samoa. The landing was hard, and a camera broke loose and struck Bean. USS Hornet picked up the crew. They went into the Mobile Quarantine Facility and remained in quarantine at Houston's Lunar Receiving Laboratory until 10 December.

The ALSEP story ran for some years. On 30 September 1977 all the remaining powered experiments were shut down, largely because of budget. Surveyor 3 is still the only probe that humans have visited on another world. Its parts were brought to Earth for study. One famous claim is that living Streptococcus mitis bacteria were found in the camera. But independent researchers challenged it. In their view the contamination probably came from a non-airtight container, or from handling the samples in a clean room after Apollo 12. So the claim is disputed.

After the mission Conrad commanded Skylab 2 and Bean commanded Skylab 3. Gordon stayed in Apollo hoping to walk on the Moon, but never flew in space again. Conrad left NASA in 1973. He later worked in business and died on 8 July 1999 from injuries in a motorcycle accident. In 2009 the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter photographed the landing site. The descent stage, ALSEP, Surveyor 3 and the footprints are still visible there. In 2011 LRO passed again at a lower altitude and returned even clearer images. So the footsteps of 1969 are still preserved in the lunar dust.

The lesson of the lightning incident was clear. An obscure switch, John Aaron's memory and Bean's recognition helped save the mission. Friends, what do you think? If you enjoyed this video, be sure to like and subscribe.

shorts.text: کیا آپ یقین کریں گے کہ ایک rocket پر دو بار بجلی گری، اور وہ پھر بھی اڑتا رہا؟ دوستو، یہ 14 November 1969 کی بات ہے۔ Apollo 12 کا Saturn V بارش میں اڑا۔ Liftoff کے 36.5 seconds بعد بجلی گری، جسے vehicle نے خود trigger کیا تھا۔ اس سے تینوں fuel cells بند ہو گئے۔ Spacecraft صرف batteries پر چل رہا تھا، مگر batteries اتنا current دے ہی نہیں سکتی تھیں۔ پھر 52 seconds پر دوسری بجلی گری۔ اس نے 8-ball attitude indicator بھی بند کر دیا۔ Astronauts کے سامنے caution اور warning lights کا پورا board سرخ تھا۔ Mission Control کی screen پر telemetry کا garbled data آ رہا تھا۔ حیرت یہ تھی کہ Saturn V پھر بھی بالکل ٹھیک اڑتا رہا۔ تو اب مسئلے کا حل کون جانتا تھا؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Kya aap yaqeen karein gay ke ek rocket par do baar bijli giri, aur woh phir bhi urta raha? Dosto, yeh 14 November 1969 ki baat hai. Apollo 12 ka Saturn V barish mein ura. Liftoff ke 36.5 seconds baad bijli giri, jise vehicle ne khud trigger kiya tha. Is se tinon fuel cells band ho gaye. Spacecraft sirf batteries par chal raha tha, magar batteries itna current de hi nahin sakti thin. Phir 52 seconds par doosri bijli giri. Is ne 8-ball attitude indicator bhi band kar diya. Astronauts ke samne caution aur warning lights ka poora board surkh tha. Mission Control ki screen par telemetry ka garbled data aa raha tha. Hairat yeh thi ke Saturn V phir bhi bilkul theek urta raha. To ab masle ka hal kaun jaanta tha? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.

Apollo 12 was struck by lightning 36.5 and 52 seconds after liftoff on 14 November 1969.
The strikes knocked the spacecraft's fuel cells offline, yet the Saturn V kept flying.

shorts.text: ایک obscure switch نے Apollo 12 کا مشن بچا لیا۔ مگر اسے جاننے والا کون تھا؟ Mission Control میں EECOM John Aaron نے یہ garbled telemetry پہلے دیکھی تھی۔ ایک earlier test میں power loss سے CSM کی signal conditioning electronics خراب ہوئی تھی۔ Aaron کو اس کا حل معلوم تھا۔ اس نے کہا: Flight, EECOM. Flight Director Gerald Griffin, CAPCOM Gerald Carr aur Conrad, tinon ko nahin maloom tha ke yeh kaun sa switch hai. Phir spacecraft ke andar ek shakhs tha jo is ki jagah jaanta tha. shorts.titleEn: Landing on the Moon Beside a Probe: Apollo 12's Pinpoint Feat
shorts.text: Conrad کو ڈر تھا کہ شاید انہیں چاند پر کچھ بھی پہچاننے کو نہ ملے۔ پھر کیا ہوا؟ 19 November 1969 کو Lunar Module Intrepid نیچے اتر رہا تھا۔ 717 seconds کا powered descent جاری تھا۔ Conrad کو training میں بتایا گیا تھا کہ pitchover کے وقت craters کا ایک pattern نظر آئے گا، جسے Snowman کہتے ہیں، اور اس کے بیچ میں Surveyor crater ہوگا۔ وہ حیران رہ گئے، کیونکہ Snowman بالکل اسی جگہ تھا۔ انہوں نے manual control سنبھالا۔ وہ Pete's Parking Lot میں اترنا چاہتے تھے، مگر وہ جگہ توقع سے زیادہ rough نکلی۔ اس لیے انہیں maneuver کرنا پڑا۔ آخرکار Intrepid اترا، Surveyor probe سے صرف 535 feet دور۔ مگر کیا دونوں astronauts اس probe تک پہنچ پائیں گے؟ پوری کہانی ہمارے channel پر دیکھیں۔
shorts.roman: Conrad ko dar tha ke shayad unhein chand par kuch bhi pehchanne ko na mile. Phir kya hua? 19 November 1969 ko Lunar Module Intrepid neeche utar raha tha. 717 seconds ka powered descent jaari tha. Conrad ko training mein bataya gaya tha ke pitchover ke waqt craters ka ek pattern nazar aaye ga, jise Snowman kehte hain, aur is ke beech mein Surveyor crater hoga. Woh hairan reh gaye, kyunke Snowman bilkul isi jagah tha. Unhon ne manual control sambhala. Woh Pete's Parking Lot mein utarna chahte thay, magar woh jagah tawaqqo se zyada rough nikli. Is liye unhein maneuver karna para. Aakhirkar Intrepid utra, Surveyor probe se sirf 535 feet door. Magar kya dono astronauts is probe tak pohanch payenge? Poori kahani hamare channel par dekhein.
shorts.descriptionEn:
On 19 November 1969 Pete Conrad spotted the Snowman craters exactly where expected and landed Intrepid 535 feet from Surveyor 3.
A pinpoint landing in the Ocean of Storms.
